verdict.reasoning: Three independent log dispatches show the same signature on three different mongodb pods within one second of each other: SIGTERM from pid 0/uid 0, orderly teardown, exit 0, silence afterwards [tr_e3f5da9a7ba3][tr_540a1d20a6c7][tr_0cd4e97940fd]. That rules out crash, OOM, saturation, replication churn and storage corruption on each instance. The synchronised timing and the single actor in the change log point to one orchestrated act affecting all six datastores, not six independent faults [tr_03f6bbb5b918][tr_044c506c1683]. Metrics could not corroborate anything: both metric dispatches failed structurally because these services emit no span-derived series, so saturation signals remain untested [tr_f427209b3657][tr_11db3f5b33a4]. The class is uncomfortable - the processes are gone rather than frozen-but-listening - but the operative fact is that the datastore processes are not running while their Services exist, and the fix is to restore the processes.
verdict.root_cause: All six mongodb instances in the hotel-reservation namespace were stopped by externally delivered SIGTERMs (kill(2), pid 0/uid 0) at 10:07:17-10:07:18, each completing a clean, fully-sequenced MongoDB shutdown with no errors and no restart afterward [tr_e3f5da9a7ba3][tr_540a1d20a6c7][tr_0cd4e97940fd]. The change log shows platform-automation provisioning these workloads fresh in the ~80 seconds before onset, including an administrative/failure-injection ConfigMap for mongodb-geo [tr_03f6bbb5b918][tr_044c506c1683]. The databases are therefore not failing-but-live: their processes are absent, so callers hit dead endpoints and the alerts at 10:08:17 reflect missing datastores rather than a defect in any one of them. The nearest fit in this taxonomy is a deliberate stop of the running artifacts, remedied by bringing the mongod processes back up.

alternatives.why_not: No mongodb log line names a bad address, credential or limit; the shutdowns are attributed to an external signal, and mongodb-reservation died identically with no ConfigMap at all [tr_044c506c1683].
alternatives.root_cause: The platform-automation provisioning burst installed an administrative/failure-injection ConfigMap whose wrong values caused the new mongodb workloads to stop serving.

alternatives.why_not: The containers are first creations with no prior version to regress from, and the processes ran normally until an external SIGTERM arrived [tr_03f6bbb5b918][tr_e3f5da9a7ba3].
alternatives.root_cause: The freshly created mongodb workloads never came up correctly - the deployed artifacts were replaced or torn down by the provisioning sequence.

open_questions: Whether the mongod processes stayed down after 10:08:23 or were restarted just outside the queried window - no startup lines were seen, but the logs were truncated.
Which actor issued the SIGTERMs; pid 0/uid 0 is consistent with kubelet pod termination but the change log does not record a delete or scale-down event.
Whether the failure-admin-geo ConfigMap drove the termination or is incidental; its contents were never read.
Whether the other three alerting datastores (profile, rate, recommendation) share the identical signature - they were never dispatched on.

draft.title: Six hotel-reservation MongoDB instances stopped by external SIGTERM

sections.body:
Six alerts arrived together at T+0, one per MongoDB instance in hotel-reservation (geo, profile, rate, recommendation, reservation, user), severity warning, with no graph-known entry point to walk back from. Six independent databases do not degrade in lockstep, so something above them acted on all of them at once.

The first move was a metrics baseline on mongodb-geo, then mongodb-user. Both came back empty, and empty in a way that is easy to misread: the backend reported the series as unavailable, not zero, because these datastores emit no traces that become Prometheus series. The whole span-derived family of queries is closed for them. Both the incident window and a separate earlier baseline failed identically, so this was not a bad time range or a transient scrape gap — retrying wider does not help. Two traps worth remembering: a blank panel here is a coverage gap, not evidence of health; and because no connection, memory, or throttling series returned either, saturation hypotheses stayed fully open at this point rather than being eliminated. Roughly twenty minutes went into this branch for no yield.
sections.heading: What was visible, and the first dead end

sections.body:
mongodb-geo received an external termination signal about a minute before the alerts and ran a complete ordered shutdown: replication step-down, three in-flight operations killed, listening sockets and connection pool closed, WiredTiger torn down, clean-shutdown marker written. Every line informational; nothing before the signal. mongodb-user matched a second later and ran the full teardown to exit status zero in about twenty-eight milliseconds, three operations in flight, no restart lines afterwards. mongodb-reservation showed the same single burst, same signal, same routine stages. In all three the signal is attributed to kill(2) from pid 0 / uid 0 — the shape of an orchestrator stopping a pod, not anything the process did to itself.

This closed several live hypotheses at once. A hard kill is excluded: it leaves no trace, whereas these teardowns completed cleanly. Connection exhaustion is excluded: no refusal or limit entries, and three in-flight operations describes a lightly loaded instance. Election churn and storage corruption are excluded: the only replication and storage entries are the normal informational shutdown stages. Caveat: the log results were truncated, so 'quiet beforehand' rests on a tail of the window.
sections.heading: Logs gave the answer in one query per service

sections.body:
The day-long change history is empty except for a tight burst by platform-automation immediately before onset. For mongodb-geo: two ConfigMaps, a Service, and the container, all created within about eighty seconds, with the container recorded as a first creation — so there was no prior running state to regress from, which closes image bumps, redeploys, sidecar changes, resource-limit tightening, node moves, and slow drift. One geo ConfigMap is named like an administrative or deliberate-failure config, created seconds before the container; its contents were never read, so it is a name, not a finding. mongodb-reservation only partially matches: Service and first container creation about a minute before onset, no ConfigMap at all. So that config is not a uniform property of the affected set. Nothing in the change log records a delete or scale-down to corroborate the terminations.

Conclusion: all six were stopped by externally delivered signals within about a second of each other; the processes are absent, so callers are hitting dead endpoints and the alerts reflect missing datastores rather than a defect in any one database. Fix class is restart. Confidence is low.

Still open: whether the processes stayed down past the window end (truncated logs, no startup lines seen — widen first); who issued the signals; what the administrative ConfigMap contains; and whether profile, rate and recommendation share the signature, since they were never examined.
sections.heading: Change log, remaining leads, and remedy

proposal.risk: If the process is being re-killed by an active injector or a controller, the restart is a no-op that costs a pod recreate and masks the real actor. If the ConfigMap-driven admin/failure config is the cause, restarting re-applies it. Any in-flight writes at recreate are lost; mongod state is on disk but in-memory sessions and caches are discarded, and the recreate is not reversible.
proposal.if_wrong: No startup lines appear, or the pod logs another SIGTERM within minutes — meaning an external agent (the suspected failure-injection path) is still stopping these processes and the restart will be undone. Note mongodb-user emits no span metrics [tr_11db3f5b33a4], so confirmation must come from logs and caller alerts, not from its own error ratio.
proposal.blast_radius: One service. Every hotel-reservation caller of mongodb-user (user/auth path) sees connection resets for the recreate duration. Five sibling datastores remain down and unaddressed by this proposal.
proposal.expected_effect: mongod is absent, not sick: SIGTERM at 10:07:18.971, clean teardown, exit 0, no startup line after. Recreating the container should yield fresh mongod startup lines in Loki for the mongodb-user pod ('Waiting for connections' on 27017) and then connection-accepted entries, within ~60s. Caller-side alerts against mongodb-user should clear.
